newsitem.title: USA: Safety officials cite propeller firm in Ga. crash.
newsitem.headline: Safety officials cite propeller firm in Ga. crash.

text.p: Federal safety officials on Tuesday accused a major propeller manufacturer of contributing to the cause of the crash of commuter plane in Georgia last year that killed eight people.

The National Transportation Safety Board cited the propeller firm, Hamilton Standard Corp., a unit of United Technologies Corp., for "inadequate and ineffectual corporation" inspection, training and other shortcomings.

It said corrosion in a blade of the type widely used on commuter planes resulted in the blade cracking, causing the Embraer EMB-120 to lose altitude quickly, forcing the pilot into a crash landing in a field near Carrollton, Georgia.
Five people on board died in the Aug. 21, 1995 crash of the Atlantic Southeast Airlines plane, operating as a Delta Air Lines Inc. commuter flight. Three died later.
The NTSA said that after blades broke off in two separate incidents in 1994, the company inspected the thousands of blades in use but its inspection was inadquate.
It said Hamilton Standard gave the work to recently hired technicians and gave them training that was inadquate to assure that blade corrosion would be discovered.

"The fracture (of the blade) was caused by a fatigue crack from multiple corrosion pits that were not discovered by Hamilton Standard because of inadequate and ineffective corporate inspection and repair techniques, training, documentation and communication," the board said.

Board chairman James Hall said the Hamilton Standard technicians were new and not adequately trained, and that while the technicians sanded off the corrosion they found, they did not find the corrosion beneath the surface.
Hall criticized the firm's "corporate culture" which pressed staff to get the propeller blades out of the inspection shops and back onto airplanes.

Shortly after the Carollton crash the Federal Aviation Administration, acting on urgent board recommendations, ordered new inspections of the blades that are used on engines on 1,800 planes worldwide, including 600 in the United States.

Hamilton Standard said in a statement that the board's findings covered its repair operations before the accident, and that since then it had acted to determine the cause of the blade fracture and to assure it did not happen again.

It said it was nearing completion of a comprehensive inspection and retrofit program fully approved by the FAA. "We are confident that this program and other actions taken since the accident have resolved the blade fracture issue."
